title: Text Adventure
summary: Build a small castle adventure from a JSON world file: rooms, items, a locked door and a goal.
brief:
Text adventures were some of the first computer games: the program describes a place, you type what to do, and it replies. In this project you'll build one from a world described in `world.json`.

You'll practise **classes**, **dictionaries**, **string handling** and **control flow**, and see how keeping data separate from code makes a program easy to extend.

datasets.description: Five rooms of a ruined castle with exits, items, one locked room and the goal.

steps.prompt: Your world lives in `world.json`: rooms with descriptions, exits, items, one locked room and a goal. You'll turn it into a playable game with **classes**, **dictionaries** and **control flow**. Run the example to see the data.
steps.exampleCode:
import json

with open("world.json") as f:
    world = json.load(f)
print(world["start"], "→ goal:", world["goal"])
for name, room in world["rooms"].items():
    print(name, sorted(room["exits"]))
steps.explanation: Every step gives you the earlier pieces, so you can focus on one new idea at a time.

steps.prompt: **Step 1 — rooms.** Write a class `Room(name, description, exits, items=None, locked_by=None)`. Store each argument as an attribute (`items` as a new list, empty if `None`). `describe()` returns three lines — the name, the description, and `Exits: ` with the exit directions sorted and joined by `, ` — plus a fourth line `You see: ` and the items when there are any.

tests.name: describe
tests.code:
r = Room('Cellar', 'Damp and dark.', {'up': 'Kitchen', 'east': 'Tunnel'})
assert r.describe() == 'Cellar\nDamp and dark.\nExits: east, up', 'describe() should give name, description and sorted exits on three lines.'

tests.name: items
tests.code:
r = Room('Shed', 'Dusty.', {'out': 'Garden'}, ['rake', 'seeds'])
assert r.describe().endswith('\nYou see: rake, seeds'), 'List the items on a last line starting You see: '

tests.name: own list
tests.code:
_items = ['rake']
r = Room('Shed', 'Dusty.', {}, _items)
r.items.append('hoe')
assert _items == ['rake'], 'Copy items into a new list so rooms do not share the caller list.'

tests.name: locked
tests.code: assert Room('Vault', 'Shiny.', {}, locked_by='key').locked_by == 'key' and Room('A', 'B', {}).locked_by is None, 'Store locked_by (None by default).'

steps.hint: Build the text with an f-string and `', '.join(sorted(self.exits))` — looping over a dictionary gives its keys.
steps.explanation: A class bundles the data about a room with the code that describes it.

steps.prompt: **Step 2 — load the world.** Write `load_world(path)` that reads the JSON file and returns a tuple `(rooms, start, goal)`: `rooms` maps each room name to a `Room`, `start` is the starting room's name and `goal` the goal dictionary.

tests.name: rooms
tests.code:
rooms, start, goal = load_world('world.json')
assert sorted(rooms) == ['Courtyard', 'Gatehouse', 'Great Hall', 'Library', 'Treasury'] and all(isinstance(r, Room) for r in rooms.values()), 'rooms should map all five names to Room objects.'

tests.name: details
tests.code:
rooms, start, goal = load_world('world.json')
assert start == 'Gatehouse' and goal == {'room': 'Treasury', 'item': 'crown'}, 'Return the start room name and the goal.'
assert rooms['Treasury'].locked_by == 'brass key' and rooms['Library'].items == ['brass key'], 'Pass items and locked_by to each Room.'
tests.message: Keep start, goal, items and locks.

steps.hint: `json.load(f)` gives nested dictionaries. Loop over `data["rooms"].items()` and use `.get()` for the optional keys.
steps.explanation: Keeping the world in a data file means you can design new adventures without touching the code.

steps.prompt: **Step 3 — understand commands.** Write `parse(command)` returning a `(verb, noun)` tuple. Ignore case and extra spaces. A direction on its own (`north`, or the short forms `n`, `s`, `e`, `w`) means `("go", direction)` with the direction written in full. Otherwise the first word is the verb and the rest (joined by single spaces) is the noun, or `None` if there's nothing else. An empty command gives `(None, None)`.

tests.name: go
tests.code: assert parse('go north') == ('go', 'north') and parse('N') == ('go', 'north') and parse('  west ') == ('go', 'west'), 'Directions should become ("go", direction).'

tests.name: nouns
tests.code: assert parse('Take   Brass Key') == ('take', 'brass key') and parse('look') == ('look', None), 'Split the verb from the rest; no noun gives None.'

tests.name: empty
tests.code: assert parse('   ') == (None, None), 'An empty command gives (None, None).'

steps.hint: `command.lower().split()` gives the words without extra spaces. A dictionary like `{"n": "north"}` handles the short forms.
steps.explanation: Normalising input first keeps the rest of the game simple.

steps.prompt: **Step 4 — moving.** Write `Player(location)` with an empty `inventory` list and `move(direction, rooms)`. If there's no exit that way, return `You can't go that way.`. If the target room has a `locked_by` item the player doesn't carry, return `The way is locked. You need the <item>.`. Otherwise move and return the new room's `describe()`.

tests.name: move
no exit
locked
tests.code:
rooms = {'A': Room('A', 'a', {'east': 'V'}), 'V': Room('V', 'v', {}, locked_by='key')}
p = Player('A')
assert p.move('east', rooms) == 'The way is locked. You need the key.' and p.location == 'A', 'A locked room needs its item.'
p.inventory.append('key')
p.move('east', rooms)
assert p.location == 'V', 'With the key, the player can enter.'

steps.hint: Check the exits first, then the lock, then move.
steps.explanation: Returning messages instead of printing them makes the game easy to test.

steps.prompt: **Step 5 — the game.** Complete `Game.handle(command)` so it understands `go` (and bare directions), `take <item>`, `look`, `inventory` (or `i`) and `quit`. Unknown verbs reply `I don't understand that.`. After any command, if the player is in the goal room holding the goal item, set `over` to `True` and add a last line `You win!`. `take` is already written.

tests.name: moves
tests.code:
g = Game('world.json')
assert g.handle('n').startswith('Courtyard') and g.handle('look').startswith('Courtyard'), 'go/directions and look should work.'

tests.name: items
tests.code:
g = Game('world.json')
assert g.handle('take lantern') == 'You take the lantern.' and g.handle('i') == 'You carry: lantern' and g.handle('take sword') == 'There is no sword here.', 'take and inventory should work.'

tests.name: unknown
tests.code:
g = Game('world.json')
assert g.handle('dance') == "I don't understand that." and g.handle('quit') == 'Bye!' and g.over, 'Handle unknown verbs and quit.'

tests.name: win
tests.code:
g = Game('world.json')
_out = [g.handle(c) for c in ['n', 'e', 'take brass key', 'w', 'n', 'e', 'take crown']]
assert _out[-1].endswith('\nYou win!') and g.over, 'Taking the crown in the Treasury should win the game.'
assert not any(o.endswith('You win!') for o in _out[:-1]), 'Only the last command should win.'

steps.hint: Call `parse`, then an `if`/`elif` chain on the verb. Check the win condition at the end, before returning.
steps.explanation: The game loop is just: read a command, update the state, reply. Everything else is data.

steps.prompt: **Step 6 — play it.** Write `play(path, commands)` that creates a `Game`, sends it each command in order and returns the list of replies, stopping as soon as the game is over (after a win or `quit`).

tests.name: win
tests.code:
_r = play('world.json', ['n', 'e', 'take brass key', 'w', 'n', 'e', 'take crown', 'look', 'look'])
assert len(_r) == 7 and _r[-1].endswith('You win!'), 'Stop as soon as the game is won.'

tests.name: locked
tests.code: assert 'locked' in play('world.json', ['n', 'n', 'e'])[-1], 'Without the key the Treasury stays locked.'

steps.explanation: To play for real on your computer, replace the list with `input()` in a `while not game.over:` loop.
